quizzes.title: 11.1 Module 11 Introduction: The Marne and the Trenches
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: The Marne and the Trenches
Survey · 2 questions · not graded
✠ ─ ✠ ─ ✠
Before you start

Welcome to The Marne and the Trenches. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Explain why Germany’s war plan depended on speed and on crossing Belgium.
  • Trace the decisions that turned the German advance into a retreat at the Marne.
  • Describe how trench warfare and attrition shaped the war after 1914.

questions.text: Before you read: Could Germany have won in 1914? Give your first answer in two or three sentences. You will answer it again at the end of the module, so it is fine if your answer changes.
I have read this module's goals and I know what I am working toward this week.

answers.text: Yes, I have read them
Not yet, I will read them before the first lesson

quizzes.title: 11.7 Reading Quiz: The Marne and the Trenches
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: The Marne and the Trenches
7 questions · 7 points
✠ ─ ✠ ─ ✠
Before you start

This quiz covers both lessons and both primary sources for this module. It has 7 questions. Most ask you to work something out from what you read, not to find a sentence in the text. You may look back at the lessons and sources while you work.

HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and keep your notes in My Notebook. Then answer the questions below.

questions.text: Why did Schlieffen’s plan send the main German army through Belgium instead of attacking France’s border head-on?

answers.text: Belgium had secretly promised to let German troops cross, so the march would meet no resistance at all
The Belgian army was too weak to put up a fight, and Germany wanted Belgian land more than a victory over France
France’s border was lined with strong forts, and a sweep through Belgium could trap the French army
Britain had told Germany it would not defend Belgium, so the German staff saw no risk in marching through it

questions.text: On August 1, 1914, the Kaiser asked whether the army could be sent east alone. Moltke said it could not. What does his answer show about the German war plan?

answers.text: Once it was set in motion it could not easily be changed
It was designed mainly to defeat Russia first and France second
It depended on the Kaiser giving orders in the field
It had been changed that week to include Belgium

questions.text: Which decision exposed the flank of the German First Army to Paris?

answers.text: Moltke’s choice to strengthen the German left wing
Hentsch’s order to retreat on September 9
Joffre’s order to fire generals who failed him
Kluck’s turn southeast to pass east of the city

questions.text: In Goschen’s report, how does Jagow’s reason for entering Belgium differ from the reason Goschen gives for Britain’s decision to go to war?

answers.text: Jagow speaks of honor and old friendship, and Goschen speaks of the speed of the German advance
Jagow calls it a matter of military need and speed, and Goschen calls it a matter of keeping a solemn promise
Both speak only of the danger from Russia, and neither of them mentions Belgium’s neutrality or any promise
Jagow denies that Belgium’s neutrality was violated, and Goschen says only that Germany had broken its word to Britain

questions.text: Why should a historian be careful about treating Goschen’s report as proof of what the chancellor really thought?

answers.text: It was written years after the war ended, when memories of the meeting had faded
Goschen was not in the room when the chancellor spoke, and had only heard the words from others afterward
A German official translated the chancellor’s words into English before Goschen wrote them down
Goschen wrote for his own government and for the British public, and he chose what to put down

questions.text: Why did some commanders come to believe in attrition?

answers.text: Frontal attacks cost huge numbers of men and gained little, so they hoped to wear the enemy down until he could not fight
They had run out of shells and could only wait for new ones to arrive from the factories at home before they tried to break through again
Their governments had agreed with one another that the war should be fought slowly, to spare the lives of the soldiers
They believed the trenches would soon be abandoned on their own once the winter weather made them too wet to hold

questions.text: In “Dulce et Decorum Est,” Owen calls the Latin line “the old Lie.” What is he arguing?

answers.text: That earlier poets had mistranslated the Latin words, so schoolboys had been taught their meaning wrongly for centuries
That the soldiers in his own army were cowards who ought to be punished for not facing the enemy as bravely as the old Roman soldiers had
That a man who had seen a death by gas could not honestly tell children that dying for one’s country is sweet and fitting
That poison gas was less deadly than most people believed, and that the dying soldier in the poem was in no real danger

discussions.title: 11.8 Discussion: Could Germany have won in 1914?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Could Germany have won in 1914?
A war plan, or the men who carried it out?
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
✠ ─ ✠ ─ ✠
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Could Germany have won in 1914?

Choose a side. In your answer, name at least two specific decisions made between 1905 and September 1914, and explain how each one could have gone another way.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on the moral side of the question. The plan required marching through a neutral country that the great powers had promised to protect. Does that bear on whether it was a good plan? Say what you think and why.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
